The Gods of the Scythians

# The Gods of the Scythians

### A people who built no temples and wrote no scripture still left us a full pantheon. Here is every god they had, and where each one actually came from.

Gold plaque of a mounted Scythian. Black Sea region, c. 400–350 BC. © The State Hermitage Museum, St Petersburg, 2017. Photo: V Terebenin.

The Scythians should not have a religion we can read.

They built no temples. Had no scripture. They raised one kind of idol only, and it was a Sword. They had no priestly class that wrote anything down, no creation hymn we can recite, no name for their own high god in their own preserved words. By every rule that lets us read a dead faith, theirs should be gone, scattered with the ash of their funeral fires across four thousand miles of Eurasian grass.

And yet we can name their gods. We can sort them. We can stand each one in a lineup and say, with reasonable confidence, this one is a cousin of the gods in the Veda, this one is a borrowed foreigner in a fresh coat of paint, this one is older than the Iranian language itself, and this one is just a Greek name thrown like a blanket over something we cannot quite see underneath.

I want to walk through the Scythian pantheon god by god, and for each one ask the only question that really matters once you have met them: where did you come from? Are you Indian, in the sense of sharing a grandparent with Agni and the waters of the Ṛgveda? Are you Iranian, a sibling of the gods Darius prayed to? Are you a deep Indo-European inheritance, as old as the word for “sky”? Are you a guest from Babylon and the Levant wearing steppe clothes? Or are you something older than all of them, something that was already haunting Siberia before a single Iranian word was spoken there?

I covered the Scythians as a people in an earlier piece, [Children of the Golden Sword](https://substack.com/@mravinderreddy/note/p-201402198?r=4pmtw8&utm_source=notes-share-action&utm_medium=web): who they were, how they fought, how they buried their kings, how they ended up in India and dissolved into it. That one had a chapter on the religion. This one is the chapter that grew into a substack piece.

## How can we know any of this?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Three witnesses let us back into a religion with no books.

The first is a Greek tourist. Around 450 BCE a man from Halicarnassus named Herodotus traveled to the Greek colonies on the north shore of the Black Sea, talked to people who dealt with Scythians every day, and wrote it all down in Book IV of his Histories. He is an outsider who never names a Scythian god in its own language without immediately translating it into a Greek one, which is a little like trying to learn Hindu theology from a visitor who insists on calling Viṣṇu “the Greek Apollo” and Śiva “their version of Dionysus.” Useful, maddening, and all we have.

The second witness is the ground itself. For two centuries archaeologists have been opening the kurgans, the great burial mounds of the steppe, and in a few miraculous cases the Siberian permafrost handed back tombs frozen whole, with the bodies, the felt, the horses, and the drug kits still inside. Again and again the excavations have confirmed the exact details that made scholars dismiss Herodotus as a fabulist. I told that story in the last piece and will not repeat it. For our purposes here the ground does one crucial thing: it proves the religion was real and practiced, not a Greek fantasy.

The third witness is the strangest and the most beautiful. High in the Caucasus mountains lives a people called the Ossetians, around two and a half million of them, who still speak an Iranian language that descends in a direct line from Scythian. Their national epic, the Nart sagas, preserves under a thin Christian glaze a pre-Christian world of gods and heroes that keeps lining up, point for point, with what Herodotus saw twenty-five centuries ago. They are as close to living Scythians as the earth still holds, and at the end of this piece they will hand us our last god, still warm.

One honest warning. Almost everything that follows is reconstruction. We are triangulating a faith from a foreign tourist, a pile of grave goods, and a poem recited three thousand miles and two and a half millennia downstream. I will flag what is solid, what is a strong scholarly bet, and what is somebody’s beautiful guess.

## The creation, in brief

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Before the pantheon there is a family tree, and it is worth one fast pass because three of our gods are born inside it.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ax35!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F826f08c3-50e3-4eb9-be50-e152f3e579d5_1516x692.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ax35!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F826f08c3-50e3-4eb9-be50-e152f3e579d5_1516x692.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The family tree of the founding myth: the sky-father Papaios (whom Herodotus calls Zeus) and the river-daughter Api give rise to Targitaos, whose three sons split the world between them. The white triangle is Kolaxais, the youngest, the only one the burning gold did not drive back, and so the king. Source: Lincoln, Once Again “the Scythian” Myth of Origins

The Scythians told it like this. The first man was Targitaos, child of the sky god and a daughter of the river. He had three sons. While they ruled, four objects of gold fell burning from the sky: a plough with its yoke, a battle-axe, and a cup. When the two elder brothers reached for the gold it blazed up and drove them back. Only when the youngest came near did the fire lie down and let itself be lifted, and so the youngest became king, and the royal line of the Scythians descended from him.

I told this story in full [last time](https://substack.com/@mravinderreddy/note/p-201402198?r=4pmtw8&utm_source=notes-share-action&utm_medium=web), including the Greek rewrite in which Herakles fathers the line on a snake legged woman, and the long scholarly fight over whether the three sons stand for the three classes of society. If you set the two family trees side by side, do not read the six names as a single lineage; they are rival casts for one plot. The Scythians’ own version makes the three brothers sons of Targitaos (Arpoxais, Lipoxais, and Kolaxais), while the Greek version gives Herakles and the snake legged queen a wholly different three (Agathyrsos, Gelonos, and Skythes). Only the shape carries across, the youngest son always taking the crown, never the names. Rather than talk about it again, here is only the part this piece needs: the receipts in the names.

The Greek rewrite of the same myth, the one the Black Sea colonists preferred: the wandering hero Herakles and a Scythian queen who is half-woman and half-viper (the snake-legged goddess) produce three sons. The shading tells the real story, white for Greek, black for Scythian, gray for the blend, and it is Skythes, the palest and so the most Greek of the three, who wins the throne. The three brothers are not random. Read through the Iranian, each is a “Lord of X,” built on the same royal word, -xšaya, “king” or “ruler,” the very word that sits inside Persian shah. Each son rules one zone of the world:

- Kolaxais, the youngest, the Sun-King

- Lipoxais, the eldest, the Lord of the mountain and the earth

- Arpoxais, the middle son, the Lord of the watery depths

Sky fire, mountain, and water: a small cosmos divided among three brothers.

And the burning gold that only the rightful king can hold has a precise Iranian name too. It is xvarǝnah, the divine radiance of legitimate kingship, the same glowing fortune that haloes kings in the Avesta, and the same word that survives in the Caucasus today as Ossetic farn, “grace” or “blessing.” A Scythian king was the man the fire did not burn. That idea is pure inherited Indo-Iranian royal ideology, and we will watch it survive to the end of the piece.

None of which means the Scythians swallowed it as innocent folklore. Bruce Lincoln, who reads origin myths as weapons rather than fairy tales, calls this one “the story Scythian kings and their apologists liked to tell,” a charter for the right to rule dressed up as a tale of falling gold.

There is one more receipt, and it points straight at India. The gifts that fell burning from the sky, the plough with its yoke, the axe, and the cup, are not random treasure. The scholar Mikhail Bukharin has argued that they are the regalia of a coronation, the same kit an Indian king handled at the rājasūya, the Vedic rite that turned a man into a king. The plough and yoke stood for the land he would break and bound; the cup held the anointing waters poured over him; the weapon marked his martial power. By taking up all of them at once, the king carried every function of society in his own body, which is exactly the claim the Scythian myth makes when only the youngest son can lift the gold. Bukharin even reaches for a particular Indian king, Pṛthu, the first sovereign ever consecrated, who took a wild and barren land, taught his people the plough, and made the earth bear fruit, the same role the Scythian heir plays when he alone can hold the fire. This is one scholar’s reconstruction and it runs out ahead of the evidence, so treat it as a strong parallel rather than a proven link. But it is the kind of parallel that does not happen twice by accident. The steppe and the Ganges were doing the same thing with the same objects, because they had inherited the same idea of what makes a king.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4cHF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4aa91b59-bf87-4881-a277-c595f59104ba_705x453.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Pṛthu chasing the Earth, who has taken the form of a cow. 18th century illustration.

Now the gods proper. Herodotus gives us the whole pantheon in a single passage, Book IV chapter 59, naming seven gods worshipped by every Scythian and an eighth reserved for the royal clan. The great Cambridge scholar Ellis Minns, whose 1913 Scythians and Greeks is still a foundation stone of the field, laid it out in one long breath:

> The following deities were common to all, Tabiti, Hestia, who was the
> principal object of their veneration, next to her Papaeus, Zeus, with
> Apia, Ge, husband and wife, after them Goetosyrus, Apollo, Argimpasa,
> Aphrodite Urania, and Ares. Thamimasadas, Poseidon, was peculiar to
> the Royal Scyths. They raised no statues, altars or temples to their
> gods, save to Ares alone.

Eight gods, one altar, no idols but a sword. We will take them in Herodotus’s order, because the order itself tells a story: he starts at the top, and the top is not where you would expect.

## 1. Tabiti, the fire-queen

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FBsd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F430c0619-974b-4089-9ea3-9cf38fd4865a_1902x1842.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FBsd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F430c0619-974b-4089-9ea3-9cf38fd4865a_1902x1842.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Scythian plaque showing a man before a deity, possibly the goddess Tabiti, 7th–3rd century BCE. The scene appears to show a male figure facing a divine or semi-divine female figure, perhaps in a ritual or offering context.

Here is the first surprise, and it is a big one. The chief deity of the Scythians, the one Herodotus says they honored above all others, the one whose name a Scythian king swore by when he wanted an oath that could not be broken, was not the thundering sky father and not the blood fed war-god. It was a goddess, and her domain was fire on the hearth.

Her name is Tabiti, and the name is a gift, because it is transparent. Strip the Greek spelling and you get something close to Tapatī, which Martin West, the Oxford philologist who mapped this entire family of gods, glosses as “the Burning one,” from an ancient root for heat and flame that runs straight through the family. The same root surfaces all over the Indian and Iranian world:

- Sanskrit tapati, “it burns” or “it glows”

- tapas, the inner heat of ascetic and ritual power that any reader of
  Indian religion knows

- the Vedic fire-god Agni and the Iranian sacred fire Ātar, her brothers
  by another name

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P_GK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5216157c-9b6e-417e-9201-2459a92e5ba2_626x883.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!P_GK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5216157c-9b6e-417e-9201-2459a92e5ba2_626x883.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The shrine of the goddess Tapati, known as the Maa Tapati Mandir ot Tapati Udgam. Multai, Madhya Pradesh, India.

She is family. When a Scythian banked the coals of the royal hearth and called them holy, he was tending the same divine fire that an Indian priest fed with ghee a thousand miles to the southeast, the two of them performing a rite they had both inherited from a common ancestor neither remembered.

A small caution, because I promised to keep the seams visible: the words being cousins does not prove the Scythians thought about fire exactly the way the Vedic tradition thought about tapas. Shared root, not shared theology. But the shared root is real, and it is the firmest etymology in the whole pantheon.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Px2m!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9c161960-823b-48a4-a942-893b572a6017_501x454.webp)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Px2m!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9c161960-823b-48a4-a942-893b572a6017_501x454.webp)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Gold plate from the Chertomlyk kurgan, possibly depicting Tabiti, the queen of the Scythian pantheon.

Then there is the puzzle that makes Tabiti genuinely strange. Across the Indo-European world the fire-god is usually male. Agni is male. Ātar is male. But the Scythian fire is a queen, and so is the Roman hearth-fire, Vesta, and so is her Greek mask here, Hestia. Something in the deep tradition let the hearth-fire be imagined as a woman, the still center of the home and the realm, while the sacrificial fire stayed a man. The Scythians, a people we picture as nothing but galloping men with bows, put a goddess of the hearth at the very top of heaven. Hold onto her. Of all eight gods in this lineup, she is the one who will still be alive at the end.

## 2. Papaios, literally “Papa”

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2PZV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F831a78f9-74f0-4ebc-af77-2bcc24300d87_500x774.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2PZV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F831a78f9-74f0-4ebc-af77-2bcc24300d87_500x774.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After the fire-queen comes the sky-father, and his name is almost too charming to be true. The Scythians called their Zeus Papaios, and Herodotus, who usually just translates a name and moves on, stops to give this one his personal endorsement. “Zeus,” he writes, “in my judgment most rightly so called, Papaeus.” The reason he approves is that Papaios is, near enough, the word “Papa.” It is the baby’s word for father, the reduplicated pa-pa that toddlers babble in language after language, promoted all the way up to the name of the highest god of the sky.

And that babble is ancient. The Indo-European sky-god was conceived as a father from the beginning, and his oldest title is exactly “Sky Father.” You can watch it surface across the whole family like the same melody played on different instruments:

- Greek Zeus patēr

- Latin Jupiter, from Dyeu-piter

- Vedic Dyaus Pitar, the Sky Father of the Ṛgveda

Papaios is that god. He is the Scythian Dyaus, the Scythian Jupiter, the bright father of the daylight sky, and his folksy nursery name is not a downgrade but a survival, the oldest and warmest thing you can call a god. The supreme being of the steppe was, to the people who feared him, just Dad.

In the creation story he is the sky half of the first divine couple, the husband of the earth. Which brings us to his wife.

## 3. Api, the earth and the waters

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qieS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6671f1b9-b64a-4ce3-a852-b81675d40d0f_454x454.webp)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qieS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6671f1b9-b64a-4ce3-a852-b81675d40d0f_454x454.webp)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Scythian kurgan figurines with phytomorphic (i.e. plant-like) or serpent feet are considered possible depictions of Api. This is from the Kul-Oba kurgan.

Papaios needs a partner, and the partnership itself is the most predictable thing in any Indo-European pantheon: Sky marries Earth, the bright father above lies with the broad mother below, and from their union the world is furnished. The Vedic poets sing of Dyaus and Pṛthivī, Heaven and Earth, as a married pair so constantly that they often fuse into a single dual word. The Scythians have the same marriage. Papaios the sky takes Api the earth, whom Herodotus matched to the Greek earth-goddess Gē, and the royal line grows from the seam where they meet.

Api’s job is clear and inherited. Her name is the knot, and the scholars split two ways on it:

- The old Soviet reading, still the popular one, takes Api from the
  Iranian āp-, “water,” making her the Earth-and-Waters and tying her
  straight to the Vedic Āpaḥ, “the Waters,” the divine female waters of
  the Ṛgveda. If that is right, she is a sister of the Indian sacred
  rivers.

- Martin West, who wrote the standard book on this material, doubts the
  water etymology and reads her name as something like “the Kindly One,”
  a respectful nickname for the earth rather than a label meaning
  Waters. He even resists calling her “Mother.”

So the verdict on Api comes in two layers. The structure, Sky-father married to Earth-mother, is rock-solid inherited Indo-European and Indo-Iranian, no argument. The name, and whether she is specifically a water-goddess and therefore a near-twin of the Vedic Āpaḥ, is genuinely unsettled. I lean toward the watery reading because it fits her partner and her people, but I am telling you it is a lean, not a proof.

## 4. Goitosyros, the cattle-lord sun

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TUc_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4104f729-5e71-4217-95e6-e8ff0241c362_1024x920.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TUc_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4104f729-5e71-4217-95e6-e8ff0241c362_1024x920.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Relief from Taq-e Bostan in Kermanshah, Iran. Ardashir II stands at the center, with Shapur II beside him and the god Mithra on the other side. Mithra is shown with rays of light radiating from his head like the sun, standing on a sacred lotus flower.

Herodotus calls him Apollo. His name says he is Mithra in disguise.

Goitosyros, sometimes written Oitosyros, is the god you would expect to know least, because he left us no myth, no recorded rite, no slab of art we can point to and say there he is. He is a name and a Greek equation, and for a long time that made him the dull cousin of the pantheon. Then you crack the name, and the dull cousin turns out to be one of the most important gods in the Iranian world wearing a false beard.

Read through the Iranian, Goitosyros resolves to something very close to Gaiϑā-sūra-, “the Mighty Lord of the Pastures,” or more bluntly, “Strong-in-Cattle.” Break the name in two:

- gaiϑā means herds, grazing land, and possessions, the wealth of a
  people who counted their fortune in livestock

- sūra- means “mighty,” the same word that turns up as the Avestan
  epithet Sūrā on the great goddess and as Vedic śūra-, “hero”

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AuHO!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F02dc257e-6d1c-4804-a429-134691de5a08_1950x950.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!AuHO!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F02dc257e-6d1c-4804-a429-134691de5a08_1950x950.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Coin of the Kushan ruler Kanishka I, featuring Miiro (Μιιρο), a form of Mithra. Dated to c. 120–150 CE.

And here is the catch that wakes the whole section up. "Mighty Lord of the Pastures" is not a generic phrase. It is a known title of Mithra, the towering Iranian god of the sun, the sworn oath, and the covenant, who carries in the Avesta the standing epithet Vouru-gaoyaoiti-, "of the Wide Pastures." The Scythian sun-god's name is, letter for letter, a Mithra epithet.

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zd5r!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8a3efb5a-2720-491b-b21d-b4a61342831f_2379x1149.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zd5r!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8a3efb5a-2720-491b-b21d-b4a61342831f_2379x1149.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Coin of Artabanus II of Parthia, dated to c. 128–124 BCE. The reverse shows the king kneeling before an Apollo-like deity, often identified as Mithra.

So the obscure one is not obscure at all in origin. He is the steppe face of Mithra, the cattle-herder's sun, the god the common Scythian who lived off his animals would have prayed to most, dressed up by Herodotus as Greek Apollo because Apollo was the Greek sun. We genuinely do not know his myths, and I will not invent them. But we know exactly where he comes from, and it is a long way from "we barely know him."

## 5. Artimpasa, the goddess in borrowed clothes

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0Su8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05be0a9b-30d9-4419-b37c-8b95a27cd1f0_1503x1046.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0Su8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F05be0a9b-30d9-4419-b37c-8b95a27cd1f0_1503x1046.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Decorated tapestry from Pazyryk Kurgan 5 in the Altai region of southern Russia, c. 241 BCE. The scene shows a seated goddess, often identified as Artimpasa, facing a Scythian rider.

If Tabiti is the surprise at the top, Artimpasa, also written Argimpasa, whom Herodotus matched to Aphrodite Ourania, the Heavenly Aphrodite, is the puzzle at the heart. She is where this religion stops looking tidy and starts looking like a real place where caravans and conquests and old local spirits all left fingerprints on the same statue. She is the great goddess, and she holds an improbable spread of powers at once:

- love and fertility

- war and sovereignty

- the wild animals, as Mistress of Beasts

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RTpr!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F692259a4-b437-4c46-8408-9999389d479c_1002x1570.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RTpr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F692259a4-b437-4c46-8408-9999389d479c_1002x1570.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Detail from the Karagodeuashkh kurgan headdress. The bottom row shows Artimpasa, seated at the center and surrounded by the Divine Twins and her attendants.

Three or four goddesses in one, which is exactly the clue to her history, because she did not start that way. She accumulated. And you can scratch down through her like coats of paint.

Start at the core. Underneath everything, Artimpasa is an Iranian goddess of the same family as Arti or Aši, the Iranian personification of fortune and reward, and she shades into the great Iranian water and fertility goddess Anāhitā, whom the Persian kings worshipped. That is her bone structure, and it is solidly Indo-Iranian. So far she is a respectable steppe relative of the Persian goddesses.

Now the borrowed coat. The Scythians of the western steppe lived next to the Greek colonies of the Black Sea, and through those colonies ran the long tendrils of the Near Eastern goddess: the armed, lion riding, sex and war goddess of the whole ancient world, called Ishtar in Babylon, Astarte by the Phoenicians, Cybele in Anatolia. Herodotus even hands us the moment of contact, and it reads like a curse out of a folktale. Generations before his own day, he says, a band of Scythians riding home from a raid into the Levant stopped at Ascalon and stripped the temple of Heavenly Aphrodite, “the most ancient,” he notes, “of all the temples of this goddess.” The goddess did not forget. She struck the robbers, and their sons, and their sons’ sons, with what Herodotus calls the “female sickness,” and the affliction ran in the blood for centuries. That temple at Ascalon was a temple of Astarte.

So in Herodotus’s own telling, the Scythian great goddess and the Levantine Ishtar-Astarte have already met, already fused, already exchanged a curse. The scholar Ustinova, who traced this overlay in detail, is admirably honest about how tangled it gets. By the time we see Artimpasa clearly, she says, it is “impossible to determine” whether a given feature of hers is Iranian, Levantine, or Greek. She is all three at once, which is what happens to a goddess who lives on a trade route.

Two borrowings shaped her most, and they are worth naming, because they explain how one goddess could hold so many jobs. From the Iranian side came Anāhitā, whose full Avestan title, Arəduuī Sūrā Anāhitā, names her three times over as the Humid, the Strong, and the Immaculate. Those three epithets are not decoration; read with Ustinova they line up with the three powers Artimpasa already carried, fertility, sovereignty, and priestly force, the whole of society folded into one figure. Anāhitā was also a patron of kings, and as she flowed into Artimpasa the Scythian goddess set hard into exactly that, the divine sponsor of the royal house who grants a man his right to rule.

From the Levantine side came something stranger, and it solves a puzzle the piece has been circling. At Ascalon the great Astarte did not stand alone; beside her was a lesser, half-bestial goddess, Atargatis, a Great Goddess shadowed by a smaller, semi-human one. Ustinova’s argument is that this pairing is the template the Scythians carried home, and that their own snake-legged foremother, human above and serpent below, slid neatly into the role of the lesser goddess attached to the greater. It lets you hold two facts at once that otherwise fight: Artimpasa and the snake-woman are almost the same figure, and yet not. Artimpasa grants the king his power and shares his bed, but she is never called the mother of the Scythians. The serpent-woman is. The borrowing shows in the seam between them.

And under even that, there is a floor. We will come back to it in the origins section, but flag it now: beneath the Iranian goddess and her Near Eastern coat lies something older still, a Mistress of the Animals descended from the deer mother of Inner Asia, the spirit who ruled the beasts long before any Iranian rode west.

She also kept the most unsettling priesthood in the ancient world, and they deserve their own section.

### The Enarei, the un-men

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c3eU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F56237788-0319-42cd-85ef-522d2a597695_1902x1364.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c3eU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F56237788-0319-42cd-85ef-522d2a597695_1902x1364.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Artist rendering of an Enaree priestess

Artimpasa was served by a class of diviners called the Enarei, and the Greeks could not stop staring at them. They were born male but lived as women, dressed as women, spoke and worked as women, and were said to have received both their changed nature and their gift of prophecy from the goddess herself. Herodotus, ever the one to reach for an embarrassing physical cause, says the goddess afflicted them with that same “female sickness” from the Ascalon curse, passing it down the generations as a kind of divine hereditary condition.

They told the future by their own peculiar method, cutting strips of lime-tree bark and braiding and unbraiding them through their fingers while they spoke the answer. The ordinary Scythian diviners read willow wands; the Enarei alone worked the linden bark, a craft the goddess was said to have handed them along with their changed bodies.

The name itself is the giveaway. Enarei comes from an Iranian phrase, a-nar-ya-, “un-manly” or “not-men.” And whatever Herodotus’s prudish medical theory, what the Enarei actually look like to a historian of religion is a recognizable type: the gender-crossing shaman-priest, the sacred third figure who is neither and both, found from the eunuch galli of Cybele in Anatolia to shamans across Siberia. They are one of the very few clearly documented cases anywhere in the ancient world of a third-gender priesthood holding real religious authority, and they belonged to the goddess of the borrowed coats, which fits, because she herself was a being who would not stay inside one category. Their very name, the un-men, will surface one last time at the end of this piece, fossilized inside a language still spoken in the mountains.

## 6. The Sword, the god you could hold

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qE-D!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5021cd50-adea-48c6-8782-672baaaf0cd8_996x994.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qE-D!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5021cd50-adea-48c6-8782-672baaaf0cd8_996x994.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The Scythians raised no statues and built no temples, with exactly one exception, and the exception is the most Scythian thing imaginable. Their war-god, whom Herodotus calls Ares, had no human image at all. He was a weapon. In each district the Scythians piled up an enormous mound of brushwood and drove into its summit a single ancient iron sword. Herodotus saw what that blade was for:

> On this pile there is set for each people an ancient scimitar of iron,
> which is their image of Ares; to this scimitar they bring yearly
> sacrifice of sheep and goats and horses.

He goes on, and it gets much darker, the wine poured over the heads of human captives and their throats cut over the iron. I staged that full rite in [Children of the Golden Sword](https://substack.com/@mravinderreddy/note/p-201402198?r=4pmtw8&utm_source=notes-share-action&utm_medium=web) and will not run the blood twice here. Remember only Minns’s dry verdict on the whole faith: they built nothing for their gods, “save to Ares alone.” Every other Scythian god was an idea. This one was an object you could pick up in your hand, and feed. What matters for the sorting is where this strange god comes from, and the answer has two parts welded together:

- The deified weapon is an inherited Indo-European pattern, not a
  Scythian eccentricity. The idea that a divine power lives inside a
  particular blade, that a sword can be a god or hold a god, runs
  through the family wherever we can see it, and at the very end of this
  piece it will give us the most famous sword in European legend.

- The war-god inside it is the specific Indo-Iranian smasher of
  resistance, the one the Avesta calls Vǝrǝθraγna (Verethragna), whose
  Ossetian descendant we are about to meet swinging a blade of tempered
  steel.

Two ancient inheritances, fused into one blade, and the only god on this whole list that could draw blood by itself.

## 7. Herakles, who is really Targitaos

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4bVd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff384045a-2d73-42cf-845d-4c3f39dd91ea_1920x1597.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4bVd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff384045a-2d73-42cf-845d-4c3f39dd91ea_1920x1597.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Herakles fighting Geryon. Greek amphora, 6th century BCE.

Herodotus lists a Scythian Herakles among the gods, and this one we can unmask quickly, because we have already met the face under the mask. The Greeks loved to find Herakles everywhere, and on the Black Sea they cheerfully made him the father of the Scythian royal line through the snake-legged woman of their preferred origin story. But the Scythians’ own first ancestor, the one who actually sat at the root of their family tree, was Targitaos, whose name reads in Iranian as something like darga-tavah-, “long-lasting strength” or “enduring power.” A good name for a progenitor.

Targitaos belongs to a recognizable Indo-Iranian type: the first man and culture-founder, the monster slaying ancestor from whom the people descend, cousin to figures like the Iranian Hušang and the dragon slayer Θraētaona of the Avesta. The Greeks looked at this powerful primordial strongman and saw their own club-swinging hero, so they called him Herakles and moved on. Peel the mask and he is the steppe’s own founding father, the human root of the genealogical myth we ran through earlier.

## 8. Thagimasadas, the royal outlier

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RCu7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa7e2d498-1390-46e3-b647-6f536688338c_960x1440.jpeg)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RCu7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa7e2d498-1390-46e3-b647-6f536688338c_960x1440.jpeg)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Poseidon greeting Theseus. c. 500–450 BCE. Now in the BnF Museum, Cabinet des Médailles, Paris.

The first seven gods belonged to all Scythians. The eighth belonged only to the Royal Scythians, the dominant tribe, and to no one else, which already makes him interesting: a god you worshipped to show which clan you were. Herodotus calls him Thagimasadas and equates him with Poseidon, god of the sea and, crucially for a horse people, god of horses. A landlocked nation of riders had no use for a sea-god, but Poseidon was also Hippios, Poseidon of the Horses, lord of the freshwater springs and the galloping herds, and that is the side of him the steppe wanted.

Thagimasadas is the hardest of the eight to pin down etymologically, and he does something structurally odd: he breaks the clean set. A pantheon of seven all-Scythian gods is a tidy, even an Iranian-feeling number, echoing the seven great holy beings of Zoroastrian Persia. Then this eighth god sticks out past the edge, belonging to one royal clan as a kind of dynastic patron of horses and waters. The best reading makes him a specifically Iranian, specifically tribal god, the divine ancestor and horse-lord of the ruling house, worshipped precisely because he was theirs and not everyone’s. Every aristocracy likes a god the commoners cannot claim.

## The faces around the edges

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Those eight are the canonical pantheon, but a few more divine figures crowd in at the margins of the sources, and they are worth a quick roll-call because each one teaches something the main eight cannot.

The snake legged goddess. A woman who is human above the waist and twin serpents below, the cave-dwelling foremother of the royal line in the Greek-flavored origin story. She may be a face of Api, or a separate chthonic ancestress, and she is everywhere in Scythian metalwork, coiled at the center of gold plaques and horse-gear. She is the one Scythian deity we can actually see, again and again, even though we are least sure of her name. Indo-Iranian ancestress under a Greek story.

The sun-god of the Massagetae. The eastern Saka people of Tomyris, the warrior queen who killed Cyrus the Great and, the story goes, dropped his severed head into a skin full of blood so the conqueror could drink his fill at last, kept the barest and cleanest religion on the steppe. Herodotus sums up their whole faith in one line: “The sun is the only god whom they worship; to him they sacrifice horses; the reason of it is that he is the swiftest of the gods, and therefore they give him the swiftest of mortal things.” That image, the sun honored with a galloping horse, is deeply Indo-Iranian: it is the same instinct behind the great Vedic horse sacrifice, the aśvamedha, where the horse is bound to the solar and royal order. Out on the far eastern edge, Tomyris and her people may have kept the oldest and barest steppe layer of all. Indo-Iranian, the eastern edition.

Ditagoia. She matters precisely because she does not fit. Centuries after Herodotus, the late Scythians who settled in the Crimea and built a small capital called Scythian Neapolis worshipped a goddess of this name, whom they equated with the Greek Artemis or the underworld Hecate. She is a different goddess wearing a different Greek mask in a different century, and she proves something important: there was never one fixed “Scythian goddess” frozen for all time. The divine feminine on the steppe kept shifting shape, absorbing whatever powerful goddess the Scythians ran into next, from Levantine Astarte in Herodotus’s day to Greek Hecate in the Crimea five hundred years later. The goddess was a sponge, and that is a fact about Scythian religion, not a flaw in our knowledge of it. A late Greek mask over a local goddess, and a lesson in how the steppe did theology.

## So where did the gods come from?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

We have met them all. Now we can answer the question the whole piece has been circling, the one a curious reader actually wants settled: taken together, is this an Indian religion, an Iranian one, a European one, a Babylonian one? The honest, satisfying answer is that it is a building with four floors, and you can name what is on each.

The first floor is inherited Indo-European, the deepest and oldest stone. The fire that is holy. The Sky-Father married to the Earth. The Father-god whose name is “Papa.” The holy weapon that holds a god. The whole habit of dividing the cosmos and society into the king, the warrior, and the producer. None of this is borrowed from anyone, because it is older than the borrowing nations existed. It is the shared inheritance the Scythians carried out of the same ancestral world that produced Greek and Latin and Sanskrit. When you feel the Ṛgveda flicker behind Tabiti and Papaios and Api, that is this floor showing through, and it is the closest the Scythians come to being “Indian,” not by descent from India but by sharing its grandparents.

The second floor is the Iranian house they actually lived in. Most of the god-names, once you crack them, are good Iranian words: the “Lord of X” princes, xvarǝnah the royal glory, a-nar-ya- the un-men, sūra- the mighty. The same gods stand in the Avesta under Persian names:

- Anāhitā behind the great goddess

- Mithra likely behind the sun

- Verethragna behind the war-god

- Ātar behind the hearth-fire

The Scythians were not generic Indo-Europeans; they were specifically Iranians, the northern cousins of the Persians, and their pantheon is an Iranian pantheon first and foremost. This is the main structure, the load-bearing one.

The third floor is a single borrowed coat, and it hangs on one figure only: the goddess. This is the cleanest and most containable part of the whole story, which is why I trust it. The Near Eastern influence, the Ishtar-Astarte-Cybele material, did not flood the pantheon. It concentrated almost entirely on Artimpasa, the Heavenly Aphrodite, picked up along the Black Sea trade routes and at temples like Ascalon. The sky-father stayed Indo-European. The fire-queen stayed Indo-Iranian. The war-sword stayed inherited. Only the great goddess put on foreign jewelry, which is exactly what great goddesses did all across the ancient world, because she was the figure most easily identified with whatever powerful goddess the next culture offered. One borrowed coat, on one shoulder.

The fourth floor is the basement, and it is older than all of them: the Siberian substrate. Before any Iranian word was spoken on this grass, Inner Asia already had its animal spirits and its deer-mother, the Mistress of the Animals who ruled the beasts. You can see her oldest monuments in the deer-stones, standing stones carved with leaping deer that radiocarbon dating places three to five centuries before the earliest Scythian art, in the Late Bronze Age cultures of Mongolia and southern Siberia that came before them.

When the Iranians rode in, they did not erase this older spirit-world; they built on top of it. The deer-mother sank down into the foundations of Artimpasa as her Mistress-of-Animals aspect, while the whole dazzling Scythian “animal style” of curled predators and folded stags kept her visual language alive on every belt and scabbard. I should flag, because honest scholars do, that whether there was one unified “Deer Goddess” is contested: some specialists see a single great animal-mother, others see only a scatter of animal spirits. But that something pre-Iranian and Siberian underlies the steppe’s sacred art is not seriously in doubt. It is the floor you stand on without noticing.

Put the four floors together and you get the real answer. Scythian religion is an Indo-Iranian system, inherited and structured, the genuine steppe sibling of the religion in the Veda and the Avesta. It wears a Near Eastern coat on the shoulders of its goddess, and it stands on a Siberian floor it never tore out. It is not Indian, exactly, and not Persian, exactly, and certainly not Greek, despite all of Herodotus’s masks. It is the third sibling, raised on the open grass between them, who kept the family fire burning in its own way.

These gods got two afterlives, and they ran in opposite directions. The eastern Saka carried the pantheon south into India, where you can watch it change religions on their own coins, a steppe war-god shading toward Śiva, a Saka dynasty endowing Buddhist monasteries within a few generations of crossing the mountains. That second life is a whole essay of its own, and it lives in [Children of the Golden Sword](https://substack.com/@mravinderreddy/note/p-201402198?r=4pmtw8&utm_source=notes-share-action&utm_medium=web) rather than here. The other afterlife, the one I want to end on, ran the opposite way, west into the mountains, and it is the stranger of the two.

## The god who is still alive

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bjwt!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F18a3c8d9-9391-4c49-beec-8e82fc398895_1102x1706.png)

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!bjwt!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F18a3c8d9-9391-4c49-beec-8e82fc398895_1102x1706.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Cover of *Tales of the Narts: Ancient Myths and Legends of the Ossetians*, translated by Walter May and edited by John Colarusso and Tamirlan Salbiev.

Religions do not usually get an epilogue. This one does.

Remember the Ossetians, our third witness, the Caucasus people who still speak a daughter of the Scythian tongue. Their Nart epic is a working museum of steppe religion. One thing to say plainly: the Nart sagas are not the Ossetians’ alone. They are the common heritage of the Caucasus, carried by the Adyghe and Kabardians, the Abkhaz, the Abazin, and the Ubykh as much as by the Ossetes, and the same heroes live on in all of them: the matriarch I call Satana is Satanaya to the Circassians and Abkhaz, and the stone-born Soslan is their Sosruko, born from the same rock in every telling.   
Vasily Abaev, who introduces the very volume I draw on here, makes the point himself: he lists these peoples one by one and insists the Narts share not a few stray motifs but one foundation, the same chief heroes under the same name, even tracing how Soslan’s name shuttled from Ossetian into Circassian, was preserved in Abkhaz, and passed back again. I dwell on the Ossetian telling for one narrow reason: Ossetic is an Iranian language descended in a straight line from Scythian, so its version preserves the linguistic thread, farn from xvarǝnah and the rest, that ties the whole epic back to the steppe. That is a reason to foreground one telling, not to erase the others. Abaev spent a lifetime laying the Scythians and the Ossetians side by side, and he caught their relationship in a single sentence: “that which with the Scythians was a living custom becomes with the Ossetians a theme for their Nart epic.” A thing that was once done in blood on the steppe survives in the mountains as a song. And the proof that this is descent and not coincidence runs through the language itself. The sound changes that turn old Scythian words into modern Ossetic are regular and traceable, so the sacred vocabulary comes through intact: xvarǝnah, the burning royal glory of the founding myth, surfaces as Ossetic farn, “divine grace,” and the a-nar-ya- “un-men” leave their mark too. The words carry the line.

And so do the gods, who walk through the Nart sagas in light disguise:

- The great goddess is still there, as Satana, the immortal mother and
  sorceress at the center of the Nart world, the wise woman without whom
  the heroes are lost. Scholars line her up with the powerful, governing
  Sarmatian and Scythian women the ancients kept reporting, the Tomyris
  type, the queen who rules.

- The sun-hero is still there, as Soslan, born miraculously from a
  stone, married to the daughter of the Sun, and killed in the end by a
  rolling solar wheel, his story still carrying buried Herodotean
  details like the warrior’s grim cloak and the straw-stuffed funeral
  horse.

- The war-god and his holy sword are there too, in the steel bodied hero
  Batraz, whose death by his own sword cast into the sea I told at the
  close of the last piece and will let that ending keep. If you have not
  read it, that is the door back to it.

But I promised you the fire-queen would outlast them all, and she does. At the top of Herodotus’s list, before the sky-father, before the sword, stood Tabiti, the hearth-fire goddess, the chief deity, the oath that could not be broken. Walk into a traditional Ossetian house twenty-five centuries later and the holiest object in it is the hearth, and above the hearth hangs an iron chain over the central fire, the rækhys. It is the most sacred thing in the home, and it governs the most charged moments of a life:

- a guest becomes sacred and untouchable the moment his hand closes on
  it

- a new bride circles it three times to enter her husband’s family

- a mother settling her child for the night keeps one hand on it and
  commends him to its keeping

To swear by it is the most binding oath a person can take; to defile it is the gravest insult a family can suffer. The Ossetians credit the chain to a hearth-god they call Safa, who gave it to humankind, but strip the later name and what you are looking at is unmistakable: the sacred hearth-fire, the unbreakable oath, the still center of the house and the realm, the very things that made Tabiti the chief god of the Scythians.

Twenty-five hundred years after a Greek tourist wrote down that the Scythians swore their deepest oaths by the royal hearth, a shepherd in the Caucasus still swears his by the chain above the fire. The sky-father faded into a folk memory. The sword-god rode off into the legend of a king and a lake. The great goddess scattered into a hundred borrowed shapes. But the fire-queen, the first name on the list, the burning one whose name is the sister of the Vedic word for sacred heat, never went out. She is the oldest thing the Scythians believed, and she is the last thing still believed, banked in the coals of a mountain house, holy, warm, and patiently waiting for the next oath.

One last honest word, because I have tried to keep the seams showing the whole way down. The match between the Narts and the Scythians is built on comparison and inference, not on a signed confession; some of the heroes’ names are borrowed from neighbors even where their stories are not, and a careful scholar holds the line that the cycles and the words carry the continuity while staying skeptical about any single tidy equation. But the fire on the hearth needs no etymology to defend it. It is just still burning, where they left it.

## Sources and further reading

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

**The ancient texts.** Herodotus, Histories, is the spine of everything here: Book IV for the pantheon list (4.59), the war-god’s sword (4.62), the founding myth (4.5 to 4.10), and the Enarei (4.67); Book I for the Ascalon curse (1.105) and the Massagetae’s sun-and-horse worship (1.216). Hippokrates, Airs, Waters, Places, adds the Enarei from the medical side. For the Iranian cousins of these gods I lean on the Avesta, above all the Ābān Yašt, which gives Anāhitā her threefold name, and the Mihr Yašt, which gives Mithra his title “lord of the wide pastures.” Quotations follow the public-domain translations of A. D. Godley and George Rawlinson.

**Reconstructing the myth and the names.** D. S. Raevsky, Scythian Mythology, is the fullest attempt to read the pantheon as one structured system. Bruce Lincoln’s essay “Once Again ‘the Scythian’ Myth of Origins” gives the skeptical, propaganda-minded reading, and supplies the two family-tree diagrams. The hard Iranian etymologies, the three “Lord of X” sons, xvarǝnah and its Ossetic survival farn, Targitaos as “enduring strength,” and Goitosyros as a Mithra epithet, come from the recent philological work of Dzitstsoyty on the Scythian language, building on Abaev and Grantovsky.

**The Indic parallels.** The bolder comparisons with the Vedic rājasūya consecration and the myth of King Pṛthu are argued by Mikhail Bukharin, “Colaxais and His Brothers.” They are a striking parallel rather than a settled fact, and I have flagged them that way in the text.

**The Indo-European frame.** M. L. West, Indo-European Poetry and Myth, is the authority for the deep-family verdicts: Tabiti as “the Burning one,” Papaios as Father Dyeus, and the cautions about Api and about over-reading trifunctional structure into the myth.

**The goddess and her borrowed coat.** Yulia Ustinova, The Supreme Gods of the Bosporan Kingdom, is the close study behind the whole Artimpasa section: the Iranian Anāhitā with her threefold name, the Levantine Astarte of Ascalon and her lesser, half-bestial twin Atargatis, and the snake-legged foremother who slid into Atargatis’s role. Ustinova is refreshingly honest that the strands are impossible to fully separate. Yuri Zaytsev, The Scythian Neapolis, covers the late Crimean goddess Ditagoia.

**The Siberian floor.** Esther Jacobson-Tepfer’s work on the deer-mother and the Mistress of the Animals, and the radiocarbon dating of the deer-stones, with the honest counter-voices who doubt a single unified “Deer Goddess.”

**The religion as lived, and the people behind it.** For the archaeology that confirms the rites, the genetics of who the Scythians were, the death-cult, the cannabis, and the Saka road into India and toward Buddhism, see my earlier piece, [Children of the Golden Sword](https://substack.com/@mravinderreddy/note/p-201402198?r=4pmtw8&utm_source=notes-share-action&utm_medium=web), and the sources gathered there (Rolle, Rudenko, Artamonov, and the recent ancient-DNA studies).

**The god still alive.** John Colarusso and Tamirlan Salbiev, Tales of the Narts, with V. I. Abaev’s introduction, is the gateway to the Ossetian survivals: Satana, Soslan, Batraz, and the sacred hearth-chain. Georges Dumézil’s lifetime of work on Scythian-to-Ossetian continuity stands behind all of it.
